title: From Submitted to Paid: What End-to-End AI Claim Follow-Up Should Actually Look Like
summary: End-to-end AI claim follow-up should move each claim toward resolution while recognizing when an account-level issue is actually a payer-wide pattern.
body_markdown:
*The objective is not to automate one more touch; it is to move the claim toward the right resolution and recognize systemic payer behavior*


**By Vanessa Couch-Laguana, Head of RCM, LunaBill**


---


Do not automate hundreds of individual calls when the real problem is a payer-wide failure to honor clean-claim payment terms.


## Start with the contract, not another phone call


If a clean claim has been submitted and is not paid within the expected timeframe, my first question is not automatically, “Who should call the payer?” My first question is, “What does the contract require?”


Prompt-payment terms should tell the organization when payment is expected for a clean claim. If those terms are being missed repeatedly, having follow-up representatives call one claim at a time may be wasted effort. The larger issue is contract performance, and the response should move to a payer-level discussion.


## Detect patterns before assigning more work


The team still plays an important role because employees often notice payer behavior first. A representative may report that claims are clean, accepted, and pending payment beyond 30 or 45 days. When several team members see the same issue, leaders should pause one-off work, pull the data, and determine whether the pattern belongs on a joint operating committee, or JOC, agenda.


This is where peer-group meetings are valuable. I recommend bringing together employees who work similar payer categories—commercial, Medicare or other government payers, behavioral health, dental, or specialty groups—at least monthly when leadership capacity allows. In a remote environment, those meetings replace the informal group sharing that once happened naturally in person. One employee can say, “I am seeing this,” and others can confirm whether they are seeing it too.


## Build the payer escalation package


Once a pattern is flagged, the analyst should pull the volume and dollars affected. Have any similar claims been paid? What is the average delay? Which claim is the oldest? Which is the highest dollar? Are certain specialties, facilities, or clinic locations disproportionately affected? How do those dates compare with the applicable contract terms?


Evidence that some comparable claims were paid can be especially useful because it shows inconsistency rather than a universal billing defect. The objective is to bring a documented issue to the payer, obtain commitment, and preserve the history so the organization can refer back to it if the behavior recurs.


## End-to-end means choosing the right level of action


An end-to-end system should check status, capture payer responses, identify missing information, recommend or execute the next appropriate step, record the action, and monitor the commitment through resolution. But it should also recognize when hundreds of claims share the same problem and stop treating them as hundreds of unrelated tasks.


Sometimes the correct next action is a portal check. Sometimes it is a payer call. Sometimes it is a corrected claim or an appeal. And sometimes it is a payer-level contract escalation supported by a JOC discussion. AI becomes more valuable when it helps the organization choose among those paths instead of simply performing more activity.
